Reproductive output in the Short-tailed bandicoot rat (Nesokia indica) has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], females can produce approximately 12 pups per year [Ri = approximately 12 pups per year], though field data suggest this can be higher under favorable conditions. Each litter typically contains three to five pups [N_R_i = Each litter typically contains three to five pups], and the interval between successive litters allows for approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year]. This moderate reproductive output is consistent with that of other murid rodents of similar body size inhabiting seasonal environments. The species' reproductive strategy appears to balance a relatively high potential fecundity against the constraints imposed by its arid and semi-arid habitats, where resource availability fluctuates markedly. Captive studies indicate that the gestation period lasts 23 days [tg = 23 days] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a figure comparable to that of the closely related black rat, Rattus rattus, upon which earlier estimates were partly based. This relatively short gestation length facilitates rapid population turnover when conditions permit.

Neonatal body mass shows considerable variation between sexes in Nesokia indica. Female newborns typically weigh approximately 4.20 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.20 grams] at birth, a modest value that underscores the altricial state of the pups. In contrast, male neonates are consistently heavier, with a recorded birth mass of 5.95 grams [Wwb = 5.95 grams]. This sex-based dimorphism at birth is noteworthy among murids and may reflect differential maternal investment or endocrine influences on fetal growth. The pups are born hairless and with closed eyes, entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition. Their rapid growth trajectory soon compensates for this low initial mass; within the first weeks of life, body weight increases substantially as the young transition from a milk-based diet to solid food. Understanding these baseline weights is essential for tracking developmental milestones and assessing the effects of environmental stressors on early survival. Field studies have confirmed similar values in wild populations, suggesting that these measurements are robust across different rearing conditions.

The developmental schedule of Nesokia indica proceeds at a predictable pace when individuals are maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Weaning, defined as the age at which pups achieve nutritional independence and no longer rely on maternal milk, occurs at 30 days after birth [tx = 30 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. At this point, the young begin to consume solid food items such as grains and seeds, though they may continue to associate with the maternal nest for several additional days. The weaning period represents a critical transition, as the juveniles must develop the foraging skills necessary for independent survival. Following weaning, the sub-adults enter a phase of rapid somatic growth and behavioral maturation. Females attain sexual maturity, marked by the first onset of estrous cycling and reproductive competence, at 140 days after birth [tp = 140 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively late pubertal development, in comparison to some other murid rodents, may be an adaptation to the unpredictable resource availability in the bandicoot rat's natural habitat, delaying reproduction until individuals have accumulated sufficient body reserves.

Adult body size in male Nesokia indica reaches a plateau that represents the species' ultimate somatic investment. The maximum recorded wet weight for adult males is 388 grams [Wwi = 388 grams], a value that places this species among the medium-to-large sized murids. This ultimate body mass is typically achieved after the completion of the rapid growth phase and the onset of reproductive activity. Males in captivity often attain this mass within their first year, whereas wild individuals may show more variability due to fluctuations in food supply and seasonal energy demands. The species exhibits a robust, thickset body plan adapted for burrowing and digging in agricultural soils, where it is considered an occasional pest. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Nesokia indica occupies an intermediate position in body size, neither as large as some African nesokiines nor as small as related Asian forms. The 388 grams adult weight is associated with a relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio, which aids in thermoregulation under the hot, arid conditions typical of its range.

Lifespan data for Nesokia indica, derived from captive colonies maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], indicate that individuals can survive for 525 days [am = 525 days], equivalent to approximately 1.4 years. This duration reflects a maximum longevity that combines a first year of adult life with an additional 160 days of extended survival under optimal conditions. In the wild, however, most individuals likely succumb to predation, disease, or seasonal resource shortages well before reaching this ceiling, with average lifespans considerably shorter. The species displays a typical rodent life history strategy characterized by high fecundity, rapid development, and relatively short generational turnover. The 525-day maximum under laboratory conditions provides a useful benchmark for demographic modeling and for comparisons with other murids occupying similar ecological niches. Periodic environmental stresses, such as drought or extreme temperatures, probably further truncate wild lifespans. Ongoing studies continue to refine these estimates by integrating longitudinal field data with captive observations to better understand the interplay between extrinsic mortality and intrinsic physiological limits.
